But Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico began making closing arguments Saturday in a tossup U.S. Senate race that has become a key measure of voters' frustration with Trump's leadership and his loyalists in the Republican Party. WATCH: Candidates make final midterm stops as early voting surges Talarico hammered Paxton, the longtime state attorney general who has weathered indictment and impeachment and garnered Trump's endorsement, as an especially corrupt example rotten political system. "This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or who puts money in his own," Talarico said in Houston. Paxton, who defeated Republican Sen. John Cornyn in this year's GOP primary with Trump's help, answered in Fort Worth by painting Talarico, a state lawmaker, seminarian and former teacher, as too liberal for Texas. And each painted the other as front men for dangerous figures. "The left in this country keeps getting more and more radical," Paxton said, arguing Talarico would be lackey for Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, the New Yorker who would set the chamber's agenda if Democrats win a majority. For Talarico, the shadow opponent is Elon Musk, the world's richest man, who has spent more than $150 million of his own money to help Paxton keep pace with Talarico's fundraising. "It's David vs. Goliath," said Talarico, invoking the biblical story of the shepherd who slays a giant. "The people of Texas are my slingshot." The closing sprint in Texas comes as early voting nears its conclusion in several states. Early balloting totals were approaching 50 million heading into the weekend. About 112 million voted in total in the 2022 midterm elections. Trump talking to voters via phone The president was stepping away from in-person rallies Saturday in favor of virtual events. He was scheduled to call into six tele-rallies after spending the morning and early afternoon at the golf club in West Palm Beach, Florida. Trump's MAGA Inc., super PAC said that telerallies were lined up for races in Pennsylvania, Ohio, New York, Michigan and two separate calls for Florida. The White House released few details on what to expect, but the president generally participates in such calls — a departure from his rally speeches, which often stretch for 90-plus minutes. "Answer your phones, and ENJOY!" Trump posted Saturday on his social media site. On Sunday, he is set to hold rallies in Iowa and Kansas that were scheduled, pulled down and then rescheduled. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who would become speaker if Democrats win a House majority, was in Virginia's 2nd Congressional District campaigning with former Rep. Elaine Luria, who is in a rematch with Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans. Luria lost her seat to Kiggans four years ago. "We're going to fight hard each and every day for an affordable America," Jeffries said. In Virginia, Jeffries previews Democratic control He hammered Republicans for filling a "graveyard of broken promises" and repeated his pledge to hold votes on reversing Republicans' healthcare cuts, pass sweeping voting rights laws and limit Trump's military actions on Iran. "Beginning on day one, we're going to hold the crooks accountable," he said, previewing aggressive oversight of the Trump administration. He specifically named Trump's Pentagon chief, Pete Hegseth, who has rankled Democrats and Republicans with his overhaul of military leadership and dismissals of top generals and other officers, among other actions. "In the majority, one of the first things we are going to do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Jeffries said, drawing perhaps the loudest roar of his 11-minute speech. The southeast Virginia district is among the most competitive in a House battleground map. Democrats are targeting at least 60 seats. Trump won many of those by double digits in 2024. Republicans lean into extreme labeling of the left House Speaker Mike Johnson answered in a Michigan tossup district with dystopian claims about Democrats. "It's a spiritual battle," the outspoken conservative Christian speaker said, suggesting Republican voters owe it to a higher power to vote. "I know God does not hold us responsible for the results, but he does hold us responsible to be faithful in our duty," Johnson said, framing Democrats as a godless party. "These are Marxists, socialists, communists. It's their ideology," he said. "The communists, as you know, murdered tens of millions of innocent people in the 20th century alone. That is not who we are in America, and it will not happen on our watch." At the same time, Trump has leaned into anti-Muslim rhetoric, focusing in particular on Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who faces Republican Mike Rogers in one of this year's most competitive Senate races. WATCH: 2026 midterms preview, plus your questions on voting On Saturday, the president posted on social media an Islamophobic cartoon of a man with a flaming torch knocking on the door of the United States after setting fire to countries in Europe. Paxton, beset by years of controversy, has followed a similar script of dire warnings and issued them again Saturday. "I'm not exaggerating when I say, if we lose Texas, we lose America," Paxton said. He urged Republicans to match enthusiastic early voting turnout from Democrats. Then he made one more entreaty. "Pray for our Texas," he said. "Pray for me." Democrats face fresh turmoil in Michigan As enthusiastic as Democrats have been about their prospects, they are still having to navigate internal divisions in El-Sayed's Michigan race. He and his former primary rival Haley Stevens were expected to campaign together on Sunday with Rep. James Clyburn, but that is in doubt. After Stevens renewed her criticism of El-Sayed, his campaign is no longer welcoming her to events, according to a person familiar with the matter who requested anonymity to discuss internal matters. However, Antjuan Seawright, a Clyburn adviser, said the congressman was still inviting both to join him for church on Sunday morning. Stevens and her spokesperson did not respond to texts asking whether she was still planning to attend. Stevens has been demanding that El-Sayed condemn an advertisement linking U.S. support for Israel to rising grocery prices and also address concerns about his past rhetoric that has concerned some Jewish voters. READ MORE: 5 expert takeaways on 2026 midterm election security Campaigning in Sterling Heights, Michigan, El-Sayed said again Saturday that "we ought to keep our money here to invest in schools here, in infrastructure here, rather than sending it somewhere else to drop a bomb somewhere else." He also alluded to how much Stevens and her supporters outspent him in the primary. "They might as well have set their money on fire, because we beat them anyway," he said. But, unlike some of his previous remarks, El-Sayed did not mention U.S. military aid to Israel or the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, and its support for Stevens and, now, Rogers. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 advantage in the Senate. Democrats need to pick up at least four new seats for a majority and would need at least five if they lose Michigan. Barrow reported from Atlanta. Associated Press reporters Joey Cappelletti and Will Weissert contributed from Washington. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. sources.news_title: Paxton and Talarico tussle for Texas Senate seat as Trump campaigns via telephone
Paxton and Talarico tussle for Texas Senate seat. Trump to campaign virtually instead of in person – WTOP News
sources.text:
Texas was not expected to be an epicenter of midterm elections that could reshape the final chapters of Donald Trump’s second presidency.
But Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico were making closing arguments Saturday in a tossup U.S. Senate race that has become a key measure of voters’ frustration with Trump’s leadership and his loyalists in the Republican Party.
Meanwhile in Michigan, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed sought to shut down talk of the intraparty conflict with his primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, calling it a distraction from issues that voters care about. The race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers for an open seat is another of this year’s most competitive contests, heightening Democratic fears about anything that could hurt the party’s chances of keeping Michigan in Democrats’ column.
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 advantage in the Senate. Democrats need to pick up at least four new seats for a majority and would need at least five if they lose Michigan.
The closing sprint comes as early voting nears its conclusion in several states. Early balloting totals were approaching 50 million heading into the weekend. About 112 million voted in total in the 2022 midterm elections.
President Donald Trump was taking a one-day break from his back-to-back rallies, instead opting to speak with voters in key states via telephone on Saturday. He’s scheduled to resume rallies on Sunday, with stops in Iowa and Kansas.
Talarico and Paxton trade jabs from afar in Texas
Speaking to voters in Houston, Talarico hammered Paxton, the longtime state attorney general who has weathered indictment and impeachment and garnered Trump’s endorsement, as an especially corrupt example of a rotten political system.
“This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or who puts money in his own,” Talarico said.
Paxton answered in Fort Worth by painting Talarico, a state lawmaker, seminarian and former teacher, as too liberal for Texas. Each painted the other as a front man for dangerous figures.
“The left in this country keeps getting more and more radical,” Paxton said, arguing Talarico would be a lackey for Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, the New Yorker who would set the chamber’s agenda if Democrats win a majority.
For Talarico, the shadow opponent is Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, who has spent more than $150 million of his own money to help Paxton keep pace with Talarico’s fundraising.
“It’s David vs. Goliath,” said Talarico, invoking the biblical story of the shepherd who slays a giant. “The people of Texas are my slingshot.”
Democrats face fresh turmoil in Michigan
As enthusiastic as Democrats have been about their prospects, they are still having to navigate internal divisions in El-Sayed’s Michigan race. He and Stevens were expected to campaign together on Sunday with Rep. James Clyburn, but that is in doubt.
Stevens has been demanding that El-Sayed condemn an advertisement linking U.S. support for Israel to rising grocery prices and also address concerns about his past rhetoric that has concerned some Jewish voters.
After Stevens renewed her criticism of El-Sayed, his campaign is no longer welcoming her to events, according to a person familiar with the matter who requested anonymity to discuss internal matters.
Antjuan Seawright, a Clyburn adviser, said the congressman was still inviting both to join him for church on Sunday morning. Stevens and her spokesperson did not respond to texts asking whether she was still planning to attend.
Speaking with reporters after a campaign stop in Sterling Heights, Michigan, El-Sayed called talk of his conflict with Stevens a distraction from the issues he wants to focus on: getting money out of politics, passing Medicare for All and putting more money in voters’ pockets.
“I’ve already been clear that that ad was not made by me and I do not agree with the contents of that ad,” El-Sayed said.
Asked whether he wants Stevens to attend church with him and Clyburn on Sunday, El-Sayed responded, “I’ve been very clear that I would rather not distract from the key issues of this campaign.” He added later that “she wants to talk about other things.”
Trump talking to voters via phone
The president was scheduled to call into six tele-rallies after spending the morning and early afternoon at the golf club in West Palm Beach, Florida.
Trump’s MAGA Inc., super PAC said that telerallies were lined up for races in Pennsylvania, Ohio, New York, Michigan and two separate calls for Florida. The White House released few details on what to expect, but the president generally participates in such calls — a departure from his rally speeches, which often stretch for 90-plus minutes.
“Answer your phones, and ENJOY!” Trump posted Saturday on his social media site.
Trump has spent the closing weeks of October traveling across the country, including in states he won comfortably in each of his three campaigns.
In Virginia, Jeffries previews Democratic control
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who would become speaker if Democrats win a House majority, was in Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District campaigning with former Rep. Elaine Luria, who is in a rematch with Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans. Luria lost her seat to Kiggans four years ago.
“We’re going to fight hard each and every day for an affordable America,” Jeffries said. He hammered Republicans for filling a “graveyard of broken promises” and repeated his pledge to hold votes on reversing Republicans’ healthcare cuts, pass sweeping voting rights laws and limit Trump’s military actions on Iran.
“Beginning on day one, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable,” he said, previewing aggressive oversight of the Trump administration.
He specifically named Trump’s Pentagon chief, Pete Hegseth, who has rankled Democrats and Republicans with his overhaul of military leadership and dismissals of top generals and other officers, among other actions.
“In the majority, one of the first things we are going to do is run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Jeffries said, drawing perhaps the loudest roar of his 11-minute speech.
The southeast Virginia district is among the most competitive in a House battleground map. Democrats are targeting at least 60 seats. Trump won many of those by double digits in 2024.
Republicans lean into extreme labeling of the left
House Speaker Mike Johnson answered in a Michigan tossup district with dystopian claims about Democrats.
“It’s a spiritual battle,” the outspoken conservative Christian speaker said, suggesting Republican voters owe it to a higher power to vote.
“These are Marxists, socialists, communists. It’s their ideology,” Johnson said.
Trump has leaned into anti-Muslim rhetoric, focusing in particular on El-Sayed. On Saturday, the president posted on social media an Islamophobic cartoon of a man with a flaming torch knocking on the door of the United States after setting fire to countries in Europe.
Paxton, beset by years of controversy, has followed a similar script of dire warnings and issued them again Saturday.
“I’m not exaggerating when I say, if we lose Texas, we lose America,” Paxton said.
“Pray for our Texas,” he said. “Pray for me.”
___ Barrow reported from Atlanta. Associated Press reporters Joey Cappelletti and Will Weissert contributed from Washington.
